concepts.def: The process in which an unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. It is a random process.
A nucleus that will give out radiation at some point because its present combination of protons and neutrons is not stable.
A process in which it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next, or when a particular nucleus will decay. Only the average behaviour of a large number of nuclei is predictable.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.
The unit in which activity is measured. One becquerel is one decay each second.
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector. It is smaller than the activity of the source, because a detector only intercepts some of the radiation emitted.
A detector of nuclear radiation. Each particle or ray it absorbs produces a pulse, and the pulses are counted to give a count-rate.
The radiation emitted by an unstable nucleus. It may be an alpha particle, a beta particle, a gamma ray or a neutron.
A particle emitted from a nucleus consisting of two neutrons and two protons; it is the same as a helium nucleus.
A high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.
Electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.
The emission of a neutron from an unstable nucleus. It is one of the types of nuclear radiation listed by the specification.
How far radiation travels into a material before it is absorbed. Alpha is stopped by paper or skin, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.
How far radiation travels through air before it is absorbed. Alpha travels a few centimetres, beta about a metre, and gamma travels a very long way.
How strongly radiation removes electrons from the atoms it passes. Alpha is the most ionising, beta is weaker, and gamma is the least ionising.
An equation used to represent radioactive decay, showing the parent nucleus on the left and the products of the decay on the right.
The top number in a nuclear symbol, giving the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. It must balance across a nuclear equation.
The bottom number in a nuclear symbol, giving the number of protons and therefore the charge of the nucleus. It must balance across a nuclear equation.
Alpha decay causes both the mass and the charge of the nucleus to decrease: the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
Beta decay does not cause the mass of the nucleus to change but does cause the charge of the nucleus to increase: the atomic number rises by 1.
The emission of a gamma ray does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change.
Choosing the mass numbers and atomic numbers so that the total mass number and the total atomic number are the same on both sides of the equation.
The time it takes for the number of nuclei of an isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate or activity from the sample to fall to half its initial level.
After n half-lives the emission has fallen by a factor of 2 to the power n, so the net decline is written as the ratio 1 : 2 to the power n.
The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. The hazard is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms.
The process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The irradiated object does not become radioactive.

Steps such as handling a source with tongs, keeping it at a distance, limiting exposure time and storing it in a lead-lined container, taken to protect against any hazard the source used for irradiation may present.
The checking of published findings by other scientists. It is why studies of the effects of radiation on humans must be published and shared.

concepts.term: Choosing a source for a use
concepts.def: Selecting the radiation whose penetration, range in air and ionising power suit the job: alpha where the radiation must be absorbed over a short distance, beta where it must pass through thin material, gamma where it must pass through thick material or out of a body.
In a nuclear equation an alpha particle may be represented by the symbol ⁴₂He, with mass number 4 written above and atomic number 2 below.
In a nuclear equation a beta particle is represented by the symbol ⁰₋₁e, with mass number 0 written above and charge −1 below.

mcqs.q: A rock sample contains unstable nuclei. Which statement best describes radioactive decay?
options: An unstable nucleus gives out radiation at random as it changes to become more stable.
Each unstable nucleus gives out its radiation at a time that can be predicted.
A nucleus gives out radiation only after the rock has been heated strongly.
Electrons dropping closer to the nucleus give out the radiation here.
mcqs.explain: Matches the specification: unstable nuclei give out radiation as they become more stable, and the process is random.

mcqs.q: A teacher says that the activity of a source is falling. What does activity mean?
options: The number of decays a nearby detector records each second.
The rate at which unstable nuclei in a source decay.
The energy released by each decay in this source.
The time in which a source fully decays away.
mcqs.explain: The specification defines activity as the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.

mcqs.q: The activity of a source is given as 480 Bq. What does the becquerel measure?
options: The energy the radiation from a source gives out each second.
The number of counts a Geiger-Muller tube records each minute.
The number of decays that happen in a source each second.
The time taken for a source to fully decay away.
mcqs.explain: One becquerel is one decay each second, so Bq measures activity.

mcqs.q: A student monitors a source with a Geiger-Muller tube. What is the count-rate?
options: The number of nuclei that decay in the whole source each second.
The energy given to the Geiger-Muller tube by radiation each second.
The number of decays the tube records, which is the activity.
The number of decays recorded each second by the detector.
mcqs.explain: The specification's definition of count-rate exactly.

mcqs.q: Which list gives the types of nuclear radiation that an unstable nucleus may emit?
options: Alpha particles, beta particles, X-rays and neutrons.
Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and neutrons.
Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and protons.
Alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays only.
mcqs.explain: These are the four emissions listed by the specification.

mcqs.q: What is an alpha particle made of?
options: Two protons and two neutrons with two electrons in orbit around them.
A single fast electron that has been thrown out of the nucleus.
Two neutrons and two protons, which is the same as a helium nucleus.
Two protons only, which is why the charge falls by two.
mcqs.explain: The specification's own description of an alpha particle.

mcqs.q: How do the properties of alpha radiation compare with those of beta and gamma?
options: It is the most penetrating radiation and travels furthest in air.
It is the least ionising but has the longest range in air.
It ionises strongly and travels several metres through the air.
It ionises most strongly and is stopped by a sheet of paper.
mcqs.explain: Alpha has the greatest ionising power, the shortest range in air and the least penetration.

mcqs.q: What is a beta particle, and where does it come from?
options: A high speed electron ejected as a neutron turns into a proton.
A high speed electron knocked out of one of the outer electron shells.
An electron that had already been stored inside the nucleus itself.
A high speed electron released as a proton turns into a neutron.
mcqs.explain: The specification's own description of a beta particle.

mcqs.q: A beta source is placed near a detector and different absorbers are tried. Which description of beta radiation is correct?
options: It is less penetrating than alpha because it is a lighter particle.
It ionises more strongly than an alpha particle and is stopped by card.
It is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium and travels about a metre in air.
It passes right through aluminium and is only reduced by thick lead.
mcqs.explain: Beta's penetration and range in air, the two properties the specification requires.

mcqs.q: What is a gamma ray?
options: A heavy particle with no charge that is thrown out of the nucleus.
Radiation given out when an electron moves between two shells.
A tiny uncharged particle shot out from inside the nucleus.
Electromagnetic radiation given out from the nucleus of an atom.
mcqs.explain: The specification's own description of a gamma ray.

mcqs.q: Which statement about gamma radiation is correct?
options: It is the least ionising radiation and the most penetrating one.
It is the most ionising radiation because it penetrates the furthest.
It is completely absorbed by a thin sheet of lead or thin concrete.
It has the shortest range in air of the three radiations.
mcqs.explain: Gamma has the lowest ionising power, the greatest penetration and the longest range in air.

mcqs.q: Some unstable nuclei emit a neutron. Which statement about this emission is correct?
options: A neutron cannot leave a nucleus, so this must really be beta decay.
A neutron (n) is one of the nuclear radiations a nucleus emits.
The neutron carries a negative charge out of the nucleus with it.
Neutron emission is another name for the release of a gamma ray.
mcqs.explain: The specification lists a neutron (n) as one of the possible emissions.

mcqs.q: In a smoke alarm the radiation crosses a small gap in air and is absorbed when smoke enters the gap. Which source is best, and why?
options: Gamma, because it is the most penetrating and always reaches the sensor.
Beta, because it goes through smoke and is easy for a detector to see.
Gamma, because alpha is too weak to cross even a small air gap.
Alpha, because it ionises strongly and is absorbed over a short range in air.
mcqs.explain: Alpha's strong ionisation and few-centimetre range mean smoke in the gap changes the reading.

mcqs.q: A paper mill measures the thickness of paper by detecting radiation that passes through it. Which source should be chosen?
options: Beta, because the amount getting through changes as the thickness changes.
Alpha, because it ionises most strongly and gives the largest reading of all.
Gamma, because it passes through the paper without being changed.
Alpha, because it is the safest radiation for the workers to be near.
mcqs.explain: Paper partly absorbs beta, so the count-rate responds to small changes in thickness.

mcqs.q: A tracer is injected into a patient and its progress is followed by a detector held outside the body. Which source is most suitable?
options: An alpha emitter, because alpha ionises most and is the easiest to detect.
A gamma emitter, because gamma passes out through the body tissue.
An alpha emitter, because paper stops alpha so it is harmless inside.
A beta emitter, because beta is stopped by skin and stays inside.
mcqs.explain: Only gamma is penetrating enough to leave the body and reach an external detector.

mcqs.q: In a nuclear equation, which symbol represents an alpha particle?
options: The symbol ²₄He, with the 2 written above the 4.
The symbol ⁰₋₁e, an electron from the nucleus.
The symbol ⁴₂He, which is a helium nucleus.
The symbol ¹₁H, which is a single proton leaving.
mcqs.explain: The specification represents an alpha particle by ⁴₂He.

mcqs.q: Which symbol is used for a beta particle in a nuclear equation?
options: ⁰₋₁e, so the mass number is 0 and the charge is −1.
⁰₊₁e, so the mass number is 0 and charge is +1.
¹₋₁e, giving a mass number of 1 and charge −1.
¹₀n, so the mass number is 1 and charge 0.
mcqs.explain: The specification represents a beta particle by ⁰₋₁e.

mcqs.q: A nucleus emits an alpha particle. How do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: The mass number falls by 2 and so does the atomic number.
The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
The mass number falls by 4 but the atomic number does not.
The mass number falls by 1 and the atomic number by 2.
mcqs.explain: Four nucleons leave, two of which are protons, so both mass and charge decrease.

mcqs.q: A nucleus emits a beta particle. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?
options: The mass falls by 1 and the charge of the nucleus increases by 1.
The mass does not change and the charge of the nucleus falls by 1.
The mass does not change but the charge increases by 1.
Both the mass and the charge of the nucleus fall by 1.
mcqs.explain: A neutron becomes a proton, so the nucleon count holds and the charge rises.

mcqs.q: When a nuclear equation for alpha decay is balanced, which quantities must be equal on both sides?
options: The number of protons only, as neutrons carry no charge.
The mass numbers only, as charge leaves with the alpha.
The number of neutrons on each side of the equation.
The total mass number and the total atomic number.
mcqs.explain: Balancing is limited to making the mass numbers and the atomic numbers match.

mcqs.q: Carbon-14 decays by beta emission: ¹⁴₆C → ᴬZ N + ⁰₋₁e. Which values of A and Z balance this equation?
options: A = 13 and Z = 7, since a particle has left the nucleus here.
A = 14 and Z = 7, since the charge rises as the mass stays the same.
A = 14 and Z = 5, since a negative particle has been lost.
A = 13 and Z = 5, since both of the numbers must fall.
mcqs.explain: Mass numbers 14 = 14 + 0 and atomic numbers 6 = 7 + (−1) both balance.

mcqs.q: A nucleus emits a gamma ray. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?
options: The mass number falls a little because energy has been carried off.
The charge falls by one but the mass number is the same.
Neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus is changed at all.
The mass number falls by four and the charge falls by two.
mcqs.explain: A gamma ray has no mass number and no charge, so both numbers are unchanged.

mcqs.q: Which statement shows that radioactive decay is a random process?
options: Each nucleus in the sample decays exactly one half-life after the last.
The decay of the sample speeds up as the number of nuclei drops.
Decay can be started or stopped by heating up the sample.
It is impossible to say which nucleus will decay next, or when.
mcqs.explain: Unpredictability of the individual event is exactly what randomness means here.

mcqs.q: The half-life of an isotope is 6 hours. What does this tell you about a sample of it?
options: In 6 hours the count rate from the sample halves.
In 6 hours every nucleus in the sample will have decayed.
In 12 hours the sample will contain no unstable nuclei.
Six hours is half the total time the sample takes to decay.
mcqs.explain: The specification defines half-life by the count rate or activity falling to half its initial level.

mcqs.q: If the decay of each nucleus is random, why does a sample have a definite half-life?
options: Because each nucleus waits its turn, so the decays are evenly spread out.
Because every nucleus is timed to decay after the same fixed period.
Because a sample holds so many nuclei that their average behaviour is predictable.
Because half of the nuclei are unstable and the other half are stable.
mcqs.explain: Large numbers make the statistics reliable even though each single event is unpredictable.

mcqs.q: The count rate from a source falls from 800 counts per second to 100 counts per second in 24 minutes. What is the half-life?
options: 24 minutes: only one halving takes place
12 minutes: half of the total time
6 minutes: 800 falls to 100 in four
8 minutes: three halvings take place
mcqs.explain: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 is three halvings in 24 minutes, so each takes 8 minutes.

mcqs.q: (HT only) The emission from a source is measured, and measured again after 4 half-lives have passed. What is the net decline, expressed as a ratio?
options: 1 : 16, as the emission halves four times over
1 : 4, as there are four half-lives in total here
16 : 1, since the emission is now sixteen times less
1 : 8, from doubling the four half-lives here
mcqs.explain: Four halvings divide the emission by 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, written 1 : 16.

mcqs.q: A worker finds radioactive dust on their overalls. Which statement describes the situation correctly?
options: This is contamination, but it is only a hazard if the dust can be seen.
This is contamination; the hazard is the decay of the dust.
This is irradiation, and the overalls have now become radioactive.
This is contamination, and the dust is a hazard by touch alone.
mcqs.explain: Contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms, and the hazard is their decay.

mcqs.q: Fruit is exposed to gamma radiation from a source in order to kill bacteria on it. What happens to the fruit?
options: The fruit becomes radioactive and must be stored before it is sold.
The fruit becomes contaminated with atoms from the gamma source.
The fruit is irradiated, so no precautions are needed by workers.
The fruit has been irradiated; it does not become radioactive itself.
mcqs.explain: Irradiation is exposure to radiation, and the irradiated object does not become radioactive.

mcqs.q: Why is an alpha emitter more hazardous inside the body than outside it?
options: Inside, its strong ionisation is absorbed by cells; outside, skin stops it.
It is never a hazard inside, because a sheet of paper is able to stop alpha.
Gamma is worse inside the body, because it passes through everything.
Alpha is only a hazard if the source is touched with bare hands.
mcqs.explain: Contamination puts the alpha source past the skin, where all of its ionising energy is absorbed.

mcqs.q: A technician uses a gamma source to irradiate surgical equipment. Which precaution is appropriate?
options: None is needed, because irradiated objects do not become radioactive.
Handle the source with tongs and store it in a lead-lined box.
Wear a paper mask, since paper is able to absorb gamma radiation.
Rinse the equipment afterwards to wash the radioactivity off.
mcqs.explain: Distance and shielding protect against the hazard the source used for irradiation presents.

mcqs.q: Studies of the effects of radiation on humans are published and shared with other scientists. Why does this matter?
options: So that members of the public can vote on whether the work is right.
So that the government decides which findings should be believed.
So that other scientists check the findings by peer review.
So that the researchers are paid for all of the work they did.
mcqs.explain: The specification requires findings to be shared so they can be checked by peer review.
